label: Big test at school

what_happens.title: What happens on test day
goals: A test shows what has been learned so far
It has instructions, questions and time
It is one day, not the whole story
what_happens.parentSkill: Explain what kind of test it is and what happens with the results.

who_is_there.title: Who is there on test day
goals: The teacher supervises and helps with instructions
Classmates are doing the same test
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child your love does not depend on the score, and say it before and after.

what_i_do.title: What I do during the test
goals: Read carefully, answer what I know first
Skip and come back to hard ones
Check my work if there is time
what_i_do.parentSkill: Teach the "know, skip, come back, check" strategy with a practice sheet.

if_scared.title: If I feel test nerves
goals: A blank mind can come back with a breath
Calm tools: breathing, skipping, positive self-talk
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the nerves and give one tool: 'Nervous is normal. If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly and skip to the next one.'

rehearsal.title: Let's get ready for the test
goals: Plan sleep, breakfast and the bag
rehearsal.parentSkill: Do a short, relaxed practice quiz with a timer, then celebrate the effort.

steps: Review a little each day before the test
Sleep well and eat breakfast on test day
Bring pencils, an eraser and a water bottle
Read each question carefully and answer the ones I know first
Come back to the hard ones and check my work
Hand in the test and take a breath
sensory: a pencil that feels sweaty in the hand
honestyNotes: Tests can feel stressful and a child may not know every answer; never promise a good grade or that it will be easy. A test measures what has been learned so far, not a child's worth. Praise preparation and effort. Let the parent say what the test is for.

fallbackAnswer: A test shows what to practise next. It does not decide who you are.
[[GROWNUP]] is proud of your effort, whatever the result.

questionButtons.text: What if my mind goes blank?
fallbackAnswer: Breathe out slowly. It often comes back.
Skip to the next question and come back later.

questionButtons.text: What if I run out of time?
fallbackAnswer: Answer what you know first, and keep an eye on the clock.
Do your best in the time you have.

questionButtons.text: What if I don't know an answer?
fallbackAnswer: Nobody knows every answer. Skip it and come back.
Make your best guess if that is allowed.
The teacher can explain the instructions or what a question means.
They cannot give answers, and that is fair for everyone.

questionButtons.text: What if my friends do better?
fallbackAnswer: Everyone is learning different things at different speeds.
Your goal is your own best, not someone else's.
Nerves are your body getting ready. Lots of kids feel them.
Slow breaths help them settle.
Tests are quiet so everyone can think.
Pencils scratching and a clock ticking are normal sounds.
Tests help teachers see what to teach next.
They also help you see how much you have learned.
[[GROWNUP]] wants to know how you felt and what you tried.
Your effort matters more than the score.

techniques.label: Know, skip, come back, check
techniques.how: Answer known questions first, skip hard ones, come back, check.

techniques.label: Short daily review
techniques.how: Review for a few minutes each day instead of cramming.

techniques.label: A practice quiz
techniques.how: Do a relaxed practice quiz with a timer at home.

techniques.label: Kind self-talk
techniques.how: Practise: I can do hard things, one question at a time.

techniques.label: Writing worries down
techniques.how: Write worries on paper for a minute before the test.

techniques.label: Sleep and breakfast
techniques.how: Go to bed early and eat a good breakfast.

techniques.label: Asking the teacher
techniques.how: Practise raising a hand to ask what a question means.

techniques.label: Praising effort
techniques.how: Praise preparation and effort, not the score.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Read, know, skip, come back, check
Hand in, big breath, well done

pain: If your head feels tight, breathe out slowly.
Take a short break and a sip of water.
body: Nerves are your body getting ready.
Sleep and breakfast help your brain.
sensory: It's quiet so everyone can think.
The clock ticking is just a clock.
strangers: The teacher can explain what a question means.
Raise your hand if you are unsure.
separation: I'll be thinking of you, and I'm proud already.
Tell me how it felt after.
unknown: Read, know, skip, come back, check.
social: Your best is what counts, not someone else's.
Lots of kids feel nervous too.
love: I love you whatever the score.
I'm proud of how you prepared.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will have a big test at school.
A test is a way for teachers to see what kids have learned so far.
It also shows what to practise next.
First [[CHILD]] sits at the desk with pencils and an eraser.
Before bed, here is a story about a young beaver called Bea.
Bea had a big building test at Beaver School.
She had to show how to build a strong little dam.
All week she practised a little each day.
On test day, she ate a good breakfast of bark.
Then Teacher Otter explained: build a dam that holds back the stream.
Bea's paws shook a bit.
She started with the part she knew best, the big logs.
Then she tried the tricky part, the mud.
When the time was up, her dam leaked a little, but it held.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Then the teacher explains the instructions.
Next everyone reads the questions and writes answers.
There is a time limit, and the teacher says how long.
Last, the tests are handed in, and it is done.
[[CHILD]] can listen carefully to the instructions and ask if something is unclear.

In the story, Bea the beaver looked around the riverbank.
Teacher Otter sat on a rock, watching the time.
If you have a question about the task, raise your paw, she said.
Next to Bea, a young muskrat was chewing his lip.
Across the stream, two beavers were whispering, quietly, no talking.
Everyone was working on their own little dam.
Bea raised her paw.
Does the dam have to be wide, she asked.
As wide as your stream, said Teacher Otter.
At home, Mama said, I am proud you tried your best.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Many of them feel nervous too.
Everyone works quietly at their own desk.

[[GROWNUP]] loves [[CHILD]] whatever the result.

During the test, [[CHILD]] reads each question carefully.
Answer the questions you know first.
If a question is hard, skip it and come back later.
Show your thinking if the test asks for it.
Watch the time, but do not rush.
[[CHILD]] can say: read, know, skip, come back, check.
In the story, Bea the beaver had a plan for the test.
Read the task twice.
Start with what you know.
Bea placed the big logs first, because she knew that well.
The mud part was hard.
Bea skipped it and did the stones next.
Then she came back to the mud, slowly, paw by paw.
Near the end, Bea checked every log.
She found one wobbly log and fixed it.
When the time was up, she took a big breath.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
If there is time at the end, check your answers.
Making a guess is better than leaving it blank, if allowed.
Then hand in the test and take a deep breath.

Step by step, it all gets a little easier.

Before a test, the tummy may feel full of butterflies.
The heart may race, and the hands may feel sweaty.
Sometimes the mind goes blank for a moment.
This is called test nerves, and lots of kids get them.
In the story, Bea the beaver felt test nerves.
Her paws felt sweaty, and her mind went blank.
I forgot everything, she whispered.
At home, Mama did not say, you will get top marks.
Mama said, nerves are normal, and a breath can bring the thinking back.
On test day, Bea remembered.
She smelled a flower slowly and blew a candle.
Then she told herself, one log at a time.
Her mind cleared, and she remembered the first step.
She kept going.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.
A slow breath helps the brain think again.
Skipping a hard question and coming back helps too.
One test does not decide how smart someone is.
Nerves usually shrink once the test starts.
[[CHILD]] can take slow breaths, smell the flower and blow the candle.
[[CHILD]] can say to themself, I can do hard things, one question at a time.

In the story, Bea the beaver got ready with Papa.
They reviewed the steps of dam building, quickly, like a song.
Logs, stones, mud, check.
Then Papa set a little sand timer for a practice.
Bea built a tiny dam with twigs.
When the twig was tricky, she skipped it and came back.
Papa clapped.
They packed her tool bag and set out bark for breakfast.
Then Papa said, sleep helps your brain hold on to things.
Bea curled up early.
And Bea slept well that night.
Next they pack the bag with pencils, an eraser and water.
After that, they plan breakfast for the morning.
Last, early to bed, because sleep helps the brain remember.
Preparing is the best way to feel ready.

Tests help teachers adjust lessons, so results guide learning, not just grades.
Standardised tests compare across many schools and are only one piece of information.
Most tests have easier and harder questions, so nobody is expected to know everything.
Good test strategy is a skill that can be learned, like reading all instructions first.
[[CHILD]] can ask the teacher what topics the test covers.
Teachers want students to show what they know, so they help with confusing wording.
Comparing scores with friends can add pressure; it is fine to keep yours private.
Some students get extra time or a quiet room if they need it, and that is fair.
A test is about the material, not about who is smart.
[[CHILD]] can talk to the teacher before the test about any worries.
Answering easy questions first builds momentum and saves time for hard ones.
Underlining key words in a question avoids misreading.
For multiple choice, crossing out wrong options improves your odds.
Checking work catches small mistakes like copying a number wrong.
[[CHILD]] can practise with a timer at home to get used to the pace.
Stress hormones can briefly block memory retrieval, which is why breathing out slowly helps unlock it.
Writing worries down for a minute before a test has been shown to improve performance.
Perfectionism makes nerves worse; aiming for your best, not perfect, helps.
If nerves feel overwhelming often, [[GROWNUP]] and the teacher can make a plan together.
[[CHILD]] can write one encouraging sentence on a sticky note to read before starting.
Spacing review over several days beats cramming the night before, because the brain stores memories while resting between sessions.
Testing yourself, like flashcards, works better than rereading notes.
Sleep consolidates memory, so staying up late can backfire.
A balanced breakfast steadies energy and focus.
[[CHILD]] can make a one-page summary of the key facts.
